case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse (via equitable doctrines such as equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions) the 30-day deadline for filing a notice of removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (the 30-day procedural time limit for removal of a civil action from state to federal court).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that district courts do have authority to excuse § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline under equitable principles in appropriate circumstances. Petitioners and supporting amici frame the deadline as a nonjurisdictional, procedural claim-processing rule that normally carries a background presumption of equitable flexibility (e.g., equitable tolling) unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise. They further argue that this case—implicating major interstate/international infrastructure, foreign-affairs sensitivities, and treaty-related issues (including arguments about the 1977 transit pipelines treaty)—presents the kind of exceptional context where federal adjudication is especially important, making an equitable exception particularly justified.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1) establishes a firm, congressionally chosen removal deadline that courts are not free to extend based on equitable considerations. Respondent and supporting amici emphasize removal’s statutory nature and the need for clear, administrable timing rules that protect state-court primacy absent timely invocation of federal jurisdiction. They contend that allowing equitable exceptions would invite uncertainty, satellite litigation, and inconsistent results, and that—at minimum—even if equitable exceptions could exist in the abstract, the circumstances here do not satisfy any demanding equitable standard. Respondent-friendly amici also urge the Court to resolve the case narrowly, potentially by holding that equitable relief is unavailable on these facts without deciding the broader question categorically.
key_precedents: Not specified in the provided excerpts (amicus briefs reference general equitable-tolling principles but the excerpts supplied do not list particular Supreme Court cases by name).

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that § 1446(b)(1) is nonjurisdictional and thus, under Irwin, presumptively subject to equitable tolling. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, the text and structure of § 1446 rebut any such presumption: Congress paired a mandatory 30-day “shall” command with specific, express timing modifications elsewhere, which leaves no textual basis for an additional, judge-made extension. And once Michigan timely invoked § 1447(c), the statute directs the consequence for this procedural defect—remand—so we should not adopt a multi-step, atextual equitable override in a scheme that reallocates cases from state to federal court. Justice Gorsuch’s administrability point further confirms that importing discretionary tolling would erode the bright-line rule Congress chose and invite satellite litigation untethered to the statute’s terms.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, so labeling § 1446(b)(1) a claim-processing rule might seem to open the door. But I agree with Justice Barrett (and the Chief) that § 1446’s interlocking timing provisions and express, enumerated exceptions rebut any inference of a free-floating equitable extension to the initial 30-day command; this is a statutory transfer mechanism where Congress’s calibrated design matters. Even if tolling were theoretically available, equitable tolling is not a roving fairness inquiry: it requires diligent pursuit and an extraordinary circumstance that actually prevented timely filing, and the asserted equities here look like forum preference rather than a Holland/Lozano-type impediment. Because Michigan timely invoked § 1447(c), the procedural defect must be enforced as written and remand follows.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that, because § 1446(b)(1) is nonjurisdictional, Irwin supplies a background presumption of equitable tolling. But as Justice Barrett explains, Congress created a detailed, interlocking timing scheme with specified escape valves—later-removal under § 1446(b)(3) and the one-year bar with a bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)(1)—which powerfully indicates Congress did not authorize an additional, open-ended equitable extension to the initial 30-day period. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that § 1447(c) makes the consequence straightforward once the plaintiff timely objects: an untimely removal is a procedural defect requiring remand, and recognizing tolling would invite administrability problems and satellite litigation inconsistent with the bright-line rule Congress chose for shifting cases from state to federal court. On these facts, the equities amount to a desire for a federal forum, not an extraordinary circumstance that actually prevented timely filing, so there is no basis to override the statutory deadline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains Irwin’s background presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, and I agree that labeling § 1446(b)(1) nonjurisdictional is not the end of the analysis. But Justice Barrett’s text-and-structure argument persuasively shows that § 1446’s interlocking timing provisions—including later-removal in § 1446(b)(3) and the one-year bar with a specific bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)(1)—rebut any inference that Congress silently authorized a free-floating tolling overlay to the basic 30-day rule. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that once Michigan timely invoked § 1447(c), the statute supplies a straightforward consequence (remand for a procedural defect), which we should not displace with an atextual equitable extension. And even if some equitable doctrines could, in theory, apply in removal, Enbridge has not identified the kind of case-specific misconduct or concealment that would support a narrower doctrine distinct from tolling on this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best shot is the Irwin/Boechler proposition that, once we classify § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day limit as nonjurisdictional, equitable tolling is presumptively available. But Justice Barrett’s text-and-structure point persuades me that this is the kind of “detailed timing architecture” that rebuts any background presumption: Congress provided specific later-removal pathways and narrowly drawn exceptions, making a judicially invented, open-ended tolling overlay look like an extra statutory exception. As the Chief Justice notes, § 1447(c) then supplies the consequence—if the plaintiff timely objects to this procedural defect, the court must remand—so we have no warrant to excuse noncompliance here. The nonjurisdictional label does real work (waiver/forfeiture), but where (as here) the objection was timely preserved, the statute’s calibrated design leaves no room for equitable enlargement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains Irwin’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling. But as Justice Barrett persuasively explains, § 1446’s detailed timing architecture—paired with express, enumerated exceptions—strongly rebuts any inference that Congress silently authorized an open-ended equitable extension to the basic 30-day command that a notice “shall” be filed within that period. In a statute that exists only by legislative grace and reallocates cases from state to federal court, separation-of-powers principles counsel against inventing a judge-made tolling regime on top of the scheme Congress wrote, and § 1447(c), as the Chief notes, makes remand the required consequence once the plaintiff timely raises this procedural defect. Whatever equities might favor a federal forum here, they are not a textual license for us to revise Congress’s deadline.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains Irwin’s general presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are subject to equitable tolling. But, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, § 1446’s interlocking timing architecture—with expressly enumerated later-removal mechanisms and specific exceptions—rebuts any inference that Congress silently authorized an additional, free-floating equitable extension of the basic 30-day clock. In this statutory, state-to-federal transfer context, administrable bright-line rules matter, and as the Chief Justice emphasizes, once the plaintiff timely raises the defect under § 1447(c), courts must enforce the claim-processing rule as written rather than layering on a discretionary, atextual tolling regime. The equities advanced by petitioner go to forum preference and policy consequences, which cannot substitute for the authority Congress did not confer in the statutory text and structure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains Irwin’s background presumption that nonjurisdictional federal filing deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, and § 1446(b)(1) is plainly nonjurisdictional. But, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the text and structure of § 1446 rebut that presumption: Congress created a calibrated timing scheme with specific later-removal pathways in § 1446(b)(3) and an express one-year bar with a bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)(1), which strongly suggests it did not invite an additional, judicially crafted “extension” of the basic 30-day clock. The Chief Justice’s point about § 1447(c) further confirms that, once a plaintiff timely raises this procedural defect, the statutory consequence is remand—so importing equitable tolling would undermine the administrable, bright-line allocation Congress chose for state-to-federal transfers. Even if tolling were conceptually available, the asserted equities here do not identify the kind of extraordinary circumstance that actually prevented timely filing under our Holland/Lozano formulation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that § 1446(b)(1) is nonjurisdictional and thus presumptively subject to equitable tolling under Irwin. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, § 1446’s interlocking timing architecture—with specific, enumerated escape valves—rebut any inference that Congress silently authorized an additional, open-ended equitable extension to the basic 30-day command. Even assuming some equitable space exists, Enbridge has not identified the kind of concrete, case-specific impediment that equity traditionally addresses (as opposed to a generalized preference for a federal forum), and Chief Justice Roberts is right that adding a discretionary overlay would erode the administrable, uniform operation Congress designed for removal. Because Michigan timely invoked the procedural defect under § 1447(c), we must enforce the claim-processing rule as written and affirm remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: By its own terms, § 1446(b)(1) sets a fixed requirement: the notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days,” and nothing in that text authorizes a court to enlarge the period based on equitable considerations. Reading an implicit equitable-tolling power into this carefully specified removal scheme would depend on a multi-step inference untethered to the statute’s language, and it would sit uneasily with Congress’s detailed timing architecture in § 1446 (including other, express timing provisions and exceptions), which is better read as leaving no free-floating equitable override. And because removal is purely statutory and affects the allocation of cases between state and federal courts, we should not infer an equitable power to extend the deadline absent a clear textual basis—particularly where § 1447(c) requires remand when a timely motion identifies a procedural defect like untimely removal. Whatever the asserted foreign-affairs or infrastructure sensitivities, they cannot supply what the statute’s text does not: an equitable exception to a congressionally chosen, administrable deadline.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days,” and in the removal context—where federal jurisdiction exists only by virtue of statute—I would read that command as a firm, administrable limit that Congress chose to protect the State’s preferred forum unless removal is timely invoked. Even if the 30-day rule is properly labeled nonjurisdictional, that does not itself authorize judge-made equitable exceptions; the availability of tolling turns on statutory intent, and the structure of the removal scheme (including § 1447(c)’s prompt remand mechanism for procedural defects) indicates Congress wanted strict, predictable timing rules rather than case-by-case excuses. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite uncertainty and collateral litigation over what counts as “exceptional,” undermining the practical benefits of a clear deadline in high-stakes disputes like this one. Whatever foreign-affairs or infrastructure interests may be implicated, it is for Congress—not courts—to create broader flexibility in removal timing, and on these facts Enbridge’s late removal cannot be excused.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, because it regulates the defendant’s removal procedure rather than the court’s adjudicatory power and appears separate from the provisions conferring removal jurisdiction. But that nonjurisdictional label does not end the inquiry: under the statutory scheme, Congress adopted a tight, mandatory 30-day window and provided specific, enumerated mechanisms for later removal in other subsections, which strongly suggests courts should enforce the 30-day bar as written when the plaintiff timely objects. Even if equitable doctrines can sometimes operate on nonjurisdictional deadlines, the open-ended equitable tolling Enbridge seeks here would effectively add an extra-statutory extension in a context where Congress prioritized administrable, predictable timing rules to protect the state forum absent prompt removal. Nor has Enbridge identified case-specific misconduct by Michigan that would fit a distinct equitable exception like equitable estoppel or fraudulent concealment, so there is no narrower equitable basis to excuse noncompliance on these facts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule: it speaks to a defendant’s obligations and sits apart from the provisions conferring removal jurisdiction, and Congress has not clearly stated that missing it strips federal courts of adjudicatory power. But once we classify it as nonjurisdictional, the next question is whether the usual presumption of equitable tolling applies—and here the statute’s structure strongly rebuts it, because Congress built a detailed removal scheme with multiple express timing modifications and exceptions (including extensions in specified contexts), signaling it did not intend an open-ended, judge-made equitable extension to the basic 30-day clock. Given that design choice and the special need for administrable, uniform rules governing the transfer of a case from state to federal court, I would hold the district court lacked authority to create an additional equitable exception on these facts. Any broader equitable arguments about the importance of a federal forum for this dispute cannot overcome Congress’s chosen, specifically calibrated timing regime.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Removal exists only by congressional authorization, and § 1446(b)(1) supplies an exception-free, mandatory 30-day instruction for when a defendant "shall" file a notice of removal after receipt of the initial pleading. Reading in equitable tolling would add a judge-made exception where the statute’s text and structure already supply carefully specified timing rules and exceptions elsewhere (e.g., later-removal in § 1446(b)(3) and the bad-faith exception to the one-year bar in § 1446(c)(1)), reinforcing that courts are not free to invent additional escape hatches. Whatever the foreign-affairs or infrastructure sensitivities here, separation of powers requires that policy arguments be directed to Congress, not used to rewrite statutory deadlines that protect state-court primacy absent timely invocation of federal jurisdiction. Because the deadline is a mandatory claim-processing rule and the equities asserted do not supply a textual basis to extend it, the district court lacks authority to excuse the untimely removal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying an institutionalist, precedent- and text-focused approach, § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline is best read as a firm claim-processing rule that courts must enforce as written, especially given removal’s strictly statutory nature and the need for clear, administrable timing rules governing the transfer of adjudicatory authority from state to federal court. The structure of the removal scheme includes multiple express timing adjustments and exceptions, which strongly suggests Congress chose when equitable flexibility is permitted and when it is not; that makes it inappropriate for courts to add an extra, atextual equitable tolling overlay. Consistent with judicial restraint and practical workability, allowing open-ended equitable exceptions would invite satellite litigation and inconsistent application in removal practice. Whatever the policy arguments about infrastructure or foreign-affairs sensitivity, those considerations do not supply a basis to depart from Congress’s calibrated deadline and exceptions in the removal statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day limit is best understood as an ordinary, nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, which would ordinarily trigger Irwin’s rebuttable presumption favoring equitable tolling. But the text-and-structure of the removal scheme rebut that presumption: Congress crafted a detailed, interlocking set of timing rules and enumerated exceptions (including specific extensions and relief mechanisms in related provisions), which strongly indicates it chose the circumstances for flexibility and foreclosed open-ended, judge-made “extensions” of the 30-day period. Allowing equitable tolling here—where removal shifts adjudicatory authority from state to federal court—would also risk the kind of uncertainty and satellite litigation that the statute’s bright-line deadlines are designed to avoid, a pragmatic consideration that reinforces the structural inference. Whatever the claimed federal interests in this dispute, they cannot supply atextual authority to enlarge a congressionally fixed removal window, and the proper course is to enforce the deadline as written.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day requirement is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, which means it is ordinarily subject to waiver/forfeiture and sometimes equitable doctrines—but only if statutory text, structure, and context indicate Congress left room for such extra-textual flexibility. Here, Michigan timely invoked the deadline via a motion to remand under § 1447(c), so the court must enforce the rule unless Congress intended equitable exceptions, and the removal scheme’s emphatic, administrable timing command (“shall be filed within 30 days”) plus Congress’s demonstrated practice of creating explicit removal exceptions (e.g., the later-enacted bad-faith exception to the one-year diversity bar) strongly suggests courts are not free to add one. On these facts, Enbridge has not shown the kind of concrete, case-specific impediment that equitable relief targets (as opposed to simply preferring a federal forum given the case’s importance), and the public-interest/systemic considerations—uniformity, predictability, and avoiding manipulation and satellite litigation in removal practice—cut against recognizing a free-floating equitable override. Accordingly, even accepting the nonjurisdictional label, I would hold equitable excusal unavailable here and affirm remand.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse (via equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions) the 30-day deadline for filing a notice of removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (30-day time limit for removal of a civil action after receipt/ service of the initial pleading); relatedly, the removal framework in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1447.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that the § 1446(b)(1) 30-day removal period is not an inflexible jurisdictional bar and that district courts retain equitable authority to excuse an untimely removal in appropriate circumstances. Petitioners and supporting amici contend that, as with most filing deadlines, Congress is presumed to incorporate equitable tolling principles absent a clear statement to the contrary; the Sixth Circuit erred by treating § 1446(b)(1) as categorically not subject to equitable exceptions. Petitioners also emphasize the case’s alleged national and international dimensions (energy infrastructure, cross-border implications, and treaty/commercial impacts) as reasons removal should be allowed notwithstanding lateness.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1) sets a mandatory procedural deadline that courts should not extend through equitable doctrines absent explicit statutory authorization, and that allowing equitable exceptions would undermine the strict, rule-like operation Congress designed for removal timing, create uncertainty, and encourage strategic delay. Respondent-supporting amici further argue that even if equitable exceptions could exist in the abstract, they are not satisfied here (i.e., Enbridge cannot show the sort of diligence and extraordinary circumstances typically required for equitable tolling) and that the Court can resolve the case without announcing a broad rule that equitable exceptions are ever available.
key_precedents: United States v. Kwai Fun Wong
Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs

John Roberts.reasoning: Even taking the strongest point from the Petitioner side—that most filing deadlines are presumed nonjurisdictional and therefore potentially subject to equitable tolling—that presumption does not supply a freestanding power to craft tolling in a tightly reticulated removal scheme. Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day rule works in tandem with § 1447(c)’s prompt-remand mechanism to produce a rule-like, speedy resolution of forum disputes; importing equitable tolling risks undermining that structure and diminishing the work done by Congress’s specific, express timing provisions and exceptions within the removal statutes. And because the Court has not squarely recognized an equitable-tolling doctrine tailored to § 1446(b)(1), I would be reluctant to announce one here absent clearer textual footing and adversarial development of its contours and limits. The pro-tolling position (as I understand Justice Gorsuch would frame it) ultimately leans more on general equitable instincts than on the particular text and interlocking design Congress enacted.
